details:
FLAMEGUARD: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data

FLAMEGUARD is a research prototype designed to support fire-safety awareness and informed decision-making during future space missions. It explores how scientific research on combustion, spacecraft fire behavior, and environmental monitoring can be brought together to help astronauts better understand potentially hazardous situations in microgravity.

The project combines two complementary capabilities: scientific evidence retrieval and environmental anomaly detection.

First, FLAMEGUARD allows users to retrieve relevant information from scientific documents and structured datasets, including PDF, CSV, and Excel files. It uses a TF-IDF-based retrieval approach to identify relevant passages and provide source references, helping users access scientific information more efficiently. When the available information is insufficient, the system is designed to acknowledge this limitation rather than provide unsupported answers.

Second, FLAMEGUARD uses an Isolation Forest model to identify unusual patterns in environmental sensor data, such as temperature variations. Its current monitoring demonstration uses synthetic sensor scenarios to illustrate how anomalies could be detected. An anomaly does not necessarily indicate a fire, and the current prototype does not predict ignition or confirm fire incidents.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Fire behavior in microgravity differs from what we observe on Earth. Understanding the relationships between temperature, oxygen, airflow, pressure, and combustible materials is therefore important for spacecraft safety research.

FLAMEGUARD aims to make relevant scientific knowledge easier to access, help identify unusual environmental patterns, and provide astronauts with evidence that can support their understanding of potentially hazardous conditions.

Its intended impact is to contribute to safer and better-informed space exploration by connecting scientific knowledge with environmental awareness and human decision support. The system is designed to assist human judgment, not replace astronauts, mission control, or approved emergency procedures.

Tools and Technologies

The current prototype uses:

  • Python: Main programming language for data processing and machine-learning components.
  • Scikit-learn: Used for TF-IDF information retrieval and the Isolation Forest anomaly-detection model.
  • Pandas: Used for processing structured datasets and tabular information.
  • PDF, CSV and Excel processing: Allows the system to ingest different scientific information formats.
  • NASA scientific resources: Including the PSI-26 BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids) investigation as part of the scientific foundation.
  • Synthetic sensor data: Used to demonstrate environmental anomaly detection without claiming access to live spacecraft telemetry.
  • Automated testing: Seven automated tests are currently reported as passing in the prototype.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of FLAMEGUARD lies in combining two different approaches that are often treated separately: scientific knowledge retrieval and environmental anomaly detection.

Rather than relying only on sensor alerts or presenting scientific documents independently, FLAMEGUARD explores how these capabilities can complement each other. When an unusual pattern is identified, relevant scientific information can help users investigate its possible context.

The project also emphasizes scientific traceability and responsible AI principles. It distinguishes between observed anomalies, scientific evidence, and unverified assumptions, while acknowledging when the available data is insufficient.

Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered several important factors:

  • Microgravity conditions: Fire behavior in space differs from combustion on Earth.
  • Scientific reliability: Information should be traceable to documented sources and experiments.
  • Data limitations: Experimental datasets and synthetic demonstrations must not be confused with real-time spacecraft measurements.
  • False alarms: An unusual sensor pattern does not automatically mean a fire is occurring.
  • Human supervision: Emergency decisions must remain under human control and follow approved procedures.
  • System limitations: Detection performance, response time, and predictive capabilities require further testing and validation.
  • Future scalability: The architecture should allow additional scientific datasets, improved retrieval methods, and more advanced monitoring capabilities to be explored.

Our long-term vision is to strengthen the scientific foundation, improve evidence retrieval and validation, advance astronaut voice interaction, and investigate how future versions could support human-supervised emergency procedures.

FLAMEGUARD's guiding idea is simple:

Read the evidence. Recognize the signals. Support safer exploration.
